Social across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

By age 5, theory of mind (everyday understanding of mental states (e.g., beliefs, intentions, knowledge) and the links between these unobservable states and action 1) is more firmly established and underpins more advanced social cognition. Five-year-olds not only understand false beliefs, but also grasp that people can have different knowledge or viewpoints on the same event. They start to comprehend that others can be fooled or surprised by things that the child himself/herself knows. They also show budding awareness of "hidden feelings"; for instance, a 5-year-old may understand that someone who is smiling could actually feel sad inside, a concept younger preschoolers struggle with. This lays the groundwork for empathy: while even toddlers exhibit basic empathic concern (e.g. distress when another child cries), 4- to 5-year-olds develop cognitive empathy (the ability to infer how someone else might feel in a given situation and why) 2. A five-year-old might say, "She’s sad because her ice cream fell," demonstrating an understanding of the connection between an event and another’s emotional state. They also start responding to others’ emotions in more appropriate ways (like offering to help or giving comfort spontaneously). Furthermore, one reputable study showed that some 5-year-olds are capable of holding meaningful values (i.e desirable goals that serve as guiding principles in a person’s life, like "having fun" or "caring for others") and can set them within a hierarchy of importance 3. A 2026 longitudinal study relates theory of mind and reasoning (Figure) 6.

Peer interactions evolve in tandem with these cognitive advances. Around 4 years, children engage in associative and cooperative play: they don’t just play side-by-side (parallel play), but actually cooperate on shared goals (building a fort together) or act out complementary roles in pretend play ("You be the doctor, I’ll be the patient"). By 5, these social play scenarios become more elaborate and governed by agreed-upon "rules" or narratives, indicating better understanding of others’ intentions and the norms of group activity. Five-year-olds are generally more cooperative and responsible than four-year-olds, often eager to please peers and adults 4. They form friendships based on shared interests and can verbalize who their "friends" are. Positive peer relationships are supported by their improved theory of mind and emotion understanding; children who can empathize and take turns tend to be well-liked, and indeed research finds that gains in ToM between 4 and 5 correlate with more positive peer interactions 5. A 2026 experiment studies social decision-making (Figure) 7.
